The vowel /o/ is always stressed. aban 'orphan' awán 'left handed' ában 'laugh' áwón 'bird' The three classes of words: noun, modifier, and verb each have their own pattern of pitch. The vowel /o/ is always stressed. aban 'orphan' | ában 'laugh' | awán 'left handed' | áwón 'bird'. The three classes of words: noun, modifier, and verb each have their own pattern of pitch. The functional load of pitch is low with only a few minimal pairs with pitch differences. [...] Tone is not written. Phonemic stress is written only when necessary.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (4 pp., PDF metadata: Author 'SIL PNG Branch', created 2004-08-19; header 'Organised Phonology Data / Faiwol Language [FAI] / Olsobip - Western Province.. Data checked by: Frank Mecklenberg (May 1992)'). Page 3, heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', reads exactly: 'Stress is contrastive on the syllable level. It is determined by length and clarity of the vowel nucleus. The vowel /o/ is always stressed.' followed by the table 'aban 'orphan' / ában 'laugh' / awán 'left handed' / áwón 'bird'' and 'The three classes of words: noun, modifier, and verb each have their own pattern of pitch. The functional load of pitch is low with only a few minimal pairs with pitch differences.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemically contrastive and not positionally predictable: disyllables contrast initial vs final stress (aban/ában, awán/áwón). The stressed syllable is the one whose vowel nucleus is longer and clearer, and /o/ always carries stress. Alongside stress, Faiwol has a marginal lexical pitch contrast (word-class-specific pitch patterns, few minimal pairs), and the primary 1974 description lists Stress (v́ vs unmarked) and Pitch (high cvc' vs unmarked low) as two separate suprasegmental phonemic units.
new_statements.exceptions: The vowel /o/ is always stressed (so words with /o/ have predictable stress); pitch differences have low functional load and are not. stress is written only when necessary.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about phonemic word/syllable-level stress in citation forms on a 4-page SIL 'Organised Phonology Data' sheet (based on Mecklenburg 1974 and the Mecklenburgs' 1969-77 manuscripts); the fuller stress and pitch sections of Mecklenburg 1974 (pp. 143-165) were not accessible, only its phoneme chart (p. 144) which confirms stress and pitch as distinct phonemic units. Healey 1964 (p. 61) independently reports contrastive lexical pitch for Angkiakmin/Faiwol.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD sheet describes Faiwol as spoken around Olsobip (villages Imigabip, Golgabip, Bolangkon, Loubip, Mikalsimbip), Western Province, i.e. Faiwol proper (faiw1243). Healey 1964's comparative data are labelled Angkiakmin (FA), a Faiwol dialect. The Setaman dialect has its own Glottolog code (seta1246) and is not the variety described here.

The vowel /o/ is always stressed.' followed by the 2x2 example block aban 'orphan' / awán 'left handed' // ában 'laugh' / áwón 'bird', then 'The three classes of words: noun, modifier, and verb each have their own pattern of pitch.' and 'The functional load of pitch is low with only a few minimal pairs with pitch differences.' The tail of the quote after '[..]' ('Tone is not. Phonemic stress is written only when necessary.') is the first…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement/type as the existing statement, which was taken from this very sheet (quote matches verbatim on p. 3). The catalog record for Faiwol (world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule field, so this statement fills it rather than contradicting it: contrastive lexical stress, conditioned by vowel length/quality with /o/ always stressed, plus low-functional-load pitch.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) at the syllable level, shown by the minimal pair aban 'orphan' vs ában 'laugh'; its placement is said to be conditioned by the length and clarity (quality) of the vowel nucleus, and /o/ is always stressed (áwón 'bird' carries two marked stresses). Alongside stress the language has pitch (tone) with low functional load: nouns, modifiers and verbs each have their own pitch pattern, and only a few minimal pairs differ by pitch. Tone is not. stress is written only when needed to disambiguate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The example áwón 'bird' is printed with an acute on both syllables, which the sheet attributes to /o/ being always stressed; no primary/secondary distinction is drawn.
new_statements.exceptions: /o/ is always stressed (a fixed quality-based exception to the lexical contrast). A vowel whose glyph dropped in text extraction (the sheet's 'Conventions: Phonological' line) 'is pronounced more central [ ] in unstressed syllables', i.e. vowel reduction in unstressed syllables. The sheet's word list and the transcribed passage are unmarked for stress and tone ('stress and tone are not marked on phonemic transcription'), so no positional generalisation over polysyllables can be extracted beyond the four examples.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Faiwol [FAI] as spoken around Olsobip, Western Province (villages Imigabip, Golgabip, Bolangkon, Loubip, Mikalsimbip; census 4,500), data checked by Frank Mecklenberg, May 1992. Healey 1964 labels the same language FA (Angkiakmin/Faiwol). Hayes & Kaun 1996 is not about any Faiwol variety; Glottolog attached it to faiw1243 by keyword ('sung').

sources.note: Comparative Ok phonology pp.60-61 gives pitch-contrast examples for FA = Angkiakmin (Faiwol) (e.g. /fim/ 'blunt' vs /bim/ 'earthquake') and states 'all the Mountain-Ok languages appear to have contrastive lexical pitch' (p.61), while calling the Faiwol/Angkiakmin phonemic description 'still rather tentative' (p.45).
